item.title: The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Achille by Glenn Adamson

Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Villa Treville Positano by Nicky Swallow and Govind Friedland

Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Mid-Century Modern Designers by Dominic Bradbury

From Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Après Ski by Erin Isakov

From cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection by A.J. Baime

Porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Wild Flowers of North America by Pamela Henson with Illustrations by Mary Vaux Walcott

Long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism by Daniel Birnbaum and Cécile Debray

For 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover by Françoise Mouly

For a century, The New Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

The Art of Korean Cooking by Onjium

Food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Football: The Ultimate Book by Alex von Kuczkowski

Not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

LIFE. Let’s Dance by Lyndsey Winship

From Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.…

item.title: A Brooklyn Exhibition Rethinks the Art of the Candleholder
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

Titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

Participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Company, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Click through the gallery above for a closer look at works featured in the exhibition.

The exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, New York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

item.title: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

When we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

1. You don’t have to know what you’re doing to get started.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

We spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”

2. Nobody has it all figured out. Seriously, nobody.

One of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

In my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”

3. The best things might be the ones you never planned.

I’m a big believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to plan? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”

4. Life gets easier and harder at the same time.

This sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”

5. Your 20s are for collecting data, not checking boxes.

My mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

My conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

We talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”

6. You have a superpower. You might just need someone else to point it out.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

In my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

If you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, new perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

item.title: Qualitative User-Research Methods: An Overview
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

This article covers 4 of the most popular qualitative-research methods: usability testing, user interview, field studies (including contextual inquiry), and diary studies.

This article is intended as a companion to Quantitative User-Research Methodologies: An Overview. As in the quant overview, we estimate the cost and difficulty of each method. These estimates are rough and relative. Your costs will depend on your tools, your participants, and how you adapt the method to your needs.

Qualitative vs Quantitative Research

Qualitative and quantitative research answer different kinds of questions:

- Qualitative research helps you understand people’s behaviors, experiences, needs, and problems. It answers why and how questions. Its findings are observations and themes, usually based on a small number of participants.

- Quantitative research measures. It reveals patterns and tells you how common a behavior or phenomenon is: how many, how much, and how often. Its findings are numbers, usually based on larger samples and analyzed with statistics.

The method alone doesn’t make a study qual or quant. Some methods, like usability testing, can be used for both. What makes the difference is your research question and how you set up the study. A qual usability test with a handful of participants looks for problems and their causes. A quant usability test with a larger sample (around 40 participants) measures metrics like success rate and time on task.

The two approaches complement each other: qual research tells you what’s happening and why, and quant research tells you how widespread it is.

Why Qualitative Research

Most UX teams run far more qualitative (qual) studies than quantitative (quant) ones, and for good reason. Qual methods are flexible, relatively inexpensive, and useful at almost any stage of a project.

But because qual methods look simple (watch a few people use your site, talk to a few more), they’re also easy to get wrong. Pick the wrong method or run the right one carelessly, and you’ll end up with misleading findings and a false sense of confidence. Done well, qual methods allow you to:

- Discover what’s wrong with a design and why.

- Understand your users’ needs, goals, pain points, and mental models before you design anything.

- See how people really behave in their own environments, including the workarounds, interruptions, and extra tools they rely on.

- Build empathy across your team. Watching a real person struggle with your product is often more persuasive than any report.

Choosing a Method

This table summarizes the methods discussed above. Costs and difficulties are general comparative estimates; ultimately, the cost of a study will depend on its goals and specific setup.

To pick the right method, lead with your research question. What do you need to know?

If you want to find problems in a design and understand why they occur, you have an evaluative question. For example:

- Do people find and understand the shipping costs before they reach checkout?

- Why are users abandoning our signup form?

- Which parts of our new prototype confuse people?

For these questions, you’ll likely want to use qualitative usability testing. (Note, if you want to measure how well a design performs, such as its success rate or time on task, you need quantitative usability testing instead.)

If you’re trying to understand people’s needs, behaviors, and experiences, you have a generative question. For example:

- What are the biggest frustrations people have when planning a vacation?

- How do nurses use patient records during a shift?

- How do people decide which meal-delivery app to use, and does that change over time?

For these questions, you’ll probably want to use user interviews, field studies, or diary studies. To choose among them, ask yourself:

- Do you need to see what people do, or is hearing about it enough? Interviews are efficient but rely on people’s memories. If accuracy about real behavior matters, observe.

- Does the environment matter? If tools, interruptions, or other people shape the experience, or if accuracy about real behavior matters, run a field study. (For complex or expert work, consider contextual inquiry.)

Does the experience unfold over days or weeks? If so, a diary study will capture it better than any single session.

Qualitative Usability Testing

- Use: Identifying problems in a design and understanding why they occur

- Cost: Low–Medium

- Difficulty of Collection: Medium

- Difficulty of Analysis: Low–Medium

- Type of Method: Behavioral (what people do)

- Context of Use: Task-based

- Typical Sample Size: About 5 participants per user group, per round of testing

In a usability test, a facilitator asks a participant to perform realistic tasks using a design, then observes what the participant does and listens to what they say. Participants are usually asked to think aloud — to narrate their thoughts as they work — so you can hear their expectations, confusion, and reasoning in the moment.

Qual and quant usability testing look alike on the surface, but they have different goals. Quant usability testing collects metrics like success rate and time on task. Qual usability testing prioritizes observations: Where did people get stuck? What did they expect to happen? Why did they choose the wrong link? Because the goal is insight, not measurement, the facilitator can ask followup questions and adjust the study as it goes.

You don’t need many participants. For a typical qual study with a single user group, testing with 5 users uncovers many of the common usability problems in a design. Testing with additional participants generally has diminishing returns, so rather than spending your budget on one big study, test with a few people, fix what you found, and test again.

Qual usability testing works at any stage, from paper prototypes to live products. You can run sessions in person, remotely with a facilitator, or remotely without one. Each format changes the cost and the amount of control you have over the session.

The biggest risk is accidentally influencing participants. Small wording problems in your tasks can prime people to look for a specific word or feature, and an untrained facilitator can change participants’ behavior by interrupting at the wrong time. Good facilitation takes practice.

For the skills you need to plan, facilitate, and analyze usability tests, see our course Usability Testing.

User Interviews

- Use: Learning about users’ experiences, needs, pain points, and motivations

- Cost: Low

- Difficulty of Collection: Medium

- Difficulty of Analysis: Medium

- Type of Method: Attitudinal (what people say)

- Context of Use: Not using product

- Typical Sample Size: Often 5–12 for a focused study; 20–30 or more for a broad one

In a user interview, the interviewer asks a participant questions about a topic, listens to their responses, and follows up to learn more. Interviews are especially useful in the discovery phase, when you’re trying to understand who your users are, what their lives are like, and what problems you could solve for them. The insights often feed into artifacts like personas and customer-journey maps.

User interviews are often confused with usability tests, but the two methods serve different purposes. A usability test evaluates a design by observing how people use it. An interview generates new knowledge about people’s experiences; participants usually don’t see or try a design at all.

A good interview is a research study, not a casual chat. Start with clear research goals, then write an interview guide with a few open-ended questions that get people talking. Ask about specific events rather than general habits. For example, Tell me about the last time you booked a vacation will produce richer, more accurate details than How do you usually book vacations? Then probe with followup questions like Tell me more about that or Why was that important to you?

How many people should you interview?…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-11-20 18:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/qual-research-methods/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=rss-syndication

item.title: Can AI Generate Good Designs from Raw User Data?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

AI can now analyze user data, provide design recommendations, and generate interfaces all in one go. So, is it still worth synthesizing research and developing recommendations first, or can teams hand AI the raw data and let it decide which user problems matter and how to solve them? The answer matters more and more as AI-generated prototypes become part of everyday design work.

To find out, we asked an AI model to generate interfaces from different types of research context. Across two design tasks, it produced better designs from synthesized findings and recommendations than from raw user comments.

About the Study

We gave an AI model two design tasks: designing a one-page form for rebooking a canceled flight and designing a multistep checkout flow for an online store. In each task, the prompt and the design-system information remained the same, while the type of research context we provided to the model changed.

While the actual study design was more complicated, in this article we will focus on two types of context that the AI model received:

- Raw user comments, which included approximately 100 comments for each design task

- Synthesized findings and recommendations based on the same raw user comments (A researcher analyzed the comments with an AI tool and made the final decisions on which findings to include and what to recommend).

Since AI tools are nondeterministic, we generated 8 designs per task and context condition. Then, a human grader and an LLM judge blindly scored each design against a predefined scorecard. The score of the design was the percentage of scorecard criteria it met (e.g., “every checkout step shows the items being bought”).

We used the human grader's scores in the results. The LLM judge scored every design independently as a check, and after calibration, the 2 graders agreed on about 96% of scoring decisions in both tasks.

Details on the study methodology are available in the accompanying sidebar.

Synthesized Findings and Recommendations Led to Better Designs

Across both design tasks, the AI-generated designs based on synthesized findings and recommendations met more scorecard criteria than designs based on raw user comments. The average difference was 8.4 percentage points and was statistically significant (p < 0.001).

The improvement was larger for the flight-rebooking task (11.4 percentage points compared to 5.5 percentage points for the checkout flow), but both tasks benefited. The finding suggests that design generation with AI can benefit from the work of synthesizing research data into findings and recommendations.

The flight-rebooking task shows what this difference looked like in practice. A few raw comments complained about loyalty miles, yet none of the designs generated from raw comments included information on whether the cancellation would affect passengers’ miles. In contrast, every design generated from synthesized research included that information.

The online-checkout task showed a smaller gain for the synthesized research but the same pattern. Several user comments complained that items disappeared from the cart during checkout, yet fewer than half of the designs based on raw data kept the items and total visible on every checkout step. Nearly all the designs made from synthesized research did. The smaller gain may be due to the task prompt, which was the same in both conditions and already pointed to some of the issues raised in the comments: It described a first-time shopper with a discount code who needed a gift within 2 days. Because the prompt itself flagged concerns such as applying a discount and receiving the order on time, even the designs made from raw comments tended to address them, leaving less room for synthesized research to make a difference.

The 8.4-percentage-point advantage of synthesized findings and recommendations may underestimate their benefit in more complex situations. First, our data was likely cleaner than typical user feedback. Although cleanliness is hard to measure, more than half of the comments in each task supported a finding, whereas research on app-store reviews found that only about a third of reviews contained information useful to product teams. Second, the dataset was small, about 100 short comments per task. Third, both tasks (designing a form and a checkout flow) are common patterns that AI models have likely seen many times. We expect the advantage of synthesized research to grow with larger, messier datasets and less familiar design problems, and we plan to study this hypothesis in the future.

Why Might Synthesized Research Improve AI-Generated Designs?

Raw Data Contains Observations Only

Raw user data describes problems, such as what frustrated users and what they wished worked differently, but it rarely says what to build in response. For example, a comment such as "Items disappeared from my cart" names a problem but does not mention a solution. Even when users suggest a fix, the suggestion isn’t a reliable guide. Users are good at describing their problems, but they’re poor at predicting what they would actually use, and what they say doesn’t always match what they do. Raw data also tends to be messy. It can include comments unrelated to the design, and different user comments may contradict each other.

Synthesized Findings and Recommendations Add a Layer of Interpretation

When working only with raw data, the AI needs to decide which data points matter and what changes to make. Those decisions are difficult because user feedback is only one input. In real life, designers weigh user feedback against business needs, technical constraints, product goals, and what the team has already tried. AI tools struggle with those tradeoffs without human guidance.

Through findings and recommendations, researchers apply their judgment to turn raw data into design decisions. They add a layer of interpretation that can help the AI generate the right design. Without them, you leave those decisions to the AI.

Findings and recommendations play different roles, though. Findings interpret the data, while recommendations turn that interpretation into design decisions. Because our analysis compared raw user comments with synthesized findings and recommendations, we don’t know at this point whether the improvements were caused by the findings or by the recommendations. We are working on determining the effect of each in a separate study.

Implications for Product Teams

Research artifacts now have two audiences: your teammates and the AI tools used in the design process. Along with artifacts created for people, we also must create artifacts that guide AI tools.

Don’t Assume Raw Research Data Is Sufficient Context

AI tools can process substantial amounts of user-research data, but that doesn't mean they will automatically identify the most important information and use it appropriately in a design. Consider what interpretation and guidance the AI tool needs rather than assuming access to the underlying data will be sufficient.

UX-Context Design: Think About What UX Knowledge AI Needs

As AI becomes more involved in generating interfaces, we will increasingly need to figure out what guidance and knowledge to provide to these tools. The context that you give an AI tool shapes what it creates. UX-context design is the practice of selecting, organizing, and maintaining the UX knowledge that guides AI-generated design. This study offers evidence that the content of this context can affect design quality.

Ongoing Research

This study raised several questions that we’re still exploring.

- Do synthesized research and recommendations improve design quality only on the specific issues addressed by the findings and recommendations, or in other respects too?

- Do the results hold for other types and larger volumes of raw data than short customer comments, such as interview transcripts, usability-test notes, or survey responses?

- Would other AI models produce the same results?…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-11-20 18:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/raw-data-vs-synthesized-data/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=rss-syndication

Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web, a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites.

The book draws on Clarke’s thirty years of web design experience. It explores how storytelling, color, typography, imagery, and layout can work together to create websites that people recognize and remember. We asked Andy a few questions about the book and the ideas that went into it.

Question: What made you want to write this book?

I’ve been designing websites for over thirty years, and I can’t remember a time when designers had more tools, techniques, and technology available to them. Yet, somehow, so many websites look remarkably similar.

I’m not suggesting every website needs a novelty design. Far from it. But I do think that — somewhere along the way—designers have become a little too comfortable with familiar patterns and predictable layouts.

I wrote Standout Designs for the Web to encourage designers to rediscover the creativity and personality that made me fall in love with the web in the first place.

Question: What’s wrong with websites looking similar? Isn’t familiarity a good thing?

Absolutely. Familiarity helps people understand how websites work, and there’s no reason to make something difficult to use just to be different. The problem is when familiarity makes every design look alike. When you visit a hotel website, an insurance company, or an online shop, you should be able to recognise something of the company behind it.

I call this sameness “commodity design,” and it’s perfectly fine when all you want is fine, but it does little to make a company recognisable or its website memorable. I’m not arguing against using conventions. I’m asking designers to make more thoughtful decisions about when to use them.

Question: You talk a lot about storytelling. What does that actually mean for web design?

When I talk about storytelling, I don’t mean writing a lengthy company history or filling a website with marketing messages.

Every company has a story worth telling. It might be how it started, the people behind it, its personality, or something unexpected about what it does. Those details can influence everything from the words you write to the colours, typography, illustrations, and layouts you choose.

I spend a lot of time talking to clients because I’m looking for what makes them different. Sometimes, something they mention almost in passing becomes the inspiration for an entire design. The trick is recognising which details are worth developing and turning them into something visual.

Question: Why did you invent a fake company for getaway drivers to demonstrate your ideas?

Ha! Because I wanted a vehicle for my explanations and to have some fun. Wheelman is a fictional company for getaway drivers, and it gave me the freedom to explore ideas without worrying too much about the practical constraints of a real client project. Its characters, criminal connections, and rather questionable business activities gave me plenty of opportunities to experiment with personality.

But there’s a serious point behind the silliness. I use Wheelman to demonstrate how a company’s character can influence ordinary business pages, e-commerce, editorial content, and even transactional forms. If I can make a donation form for retired criminals interesting, designers have no reason not to bring more personality to everyday websites.

Question: You challenge the twelve-column grid. Have designers become too dependent on it?

I think twelve-column grids have become the default setting for web design. They’re familiar and useful, but they’re only one way to organise content. When designers begin every project with twelve columns, they’re already limiting their possibilities before they’ve considered what the content needs.

In the book, I explore column, compound, and modular grids; ratios; symmetry versus asymmetry; and other ways to create rhythm and movement across a page. I’m not suggesting designers abandon column grids, but I want them to understand layout well enough to choose the right type and combine several—to make their layouts more interesting.

Question: What’s the one thing you’d like someone to do differently after reading your book?

I’d like them to approach their next project with a little more curiosity. Before opening Figma or Sketch, choosing a typeface, or deciding on a layout, I’d like them to spend more time discovering what makes the company they’re designing for interesting.

Then I’d encourage them to question their first design decisions. Does this layout suit the content, or is it just familiar? Does this typography express the company’s personality? Can an illustration communicate something more effectively than an AI-generated image or a stock photo?

I don’t expect every website to be extraordinary, and I certainly don’t think every design needs to break conventions. But I’d like designers to feel more confident making decisions that give their work character.
